parole.significato: Pertaining to a tail-like structure.
parole.testo: From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: shinned
parole.testo: From New Latin cnēmis, from Ancient Greek κνήμη (knḗmē, “shin”) + -ic.

parole.significato: any spherical microorganism
parole.testo: From New Latin coccus, from Latin coccum, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).

parole.significato: Denoting diseases characterized by inflammation, itself often caused by an infection.
parole.testo: From New Latin -itis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”). This is the feminine form of adjectival suffix -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). parole.significato: Word.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ὄνυμα (ónuma), Doric and Aeolic dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”); compare also -onymy § Etymology.

parole.significato: functional disease or condition such as hepatosis
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -ōsis, from Ancient Greek -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”), from -όω (-óō) stem verbs + -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: Synonym of -phasia: forms names of speech disorders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin -phēmia, from Ancient Greek φήμη (phḗmē, “voice”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin, from Ancient Greek -φοβία (-phobía), from φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Bearer, carrier or conveyor.
parole.testo: From New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”). See phoresy.

parole.significato: Growth or formation
parole.testo: From New Latin -plasia, from Ancient Greek πλάσις (plásis, “molding, formation”).

parole.significato: rupture
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥῆξις (rhêxis), from ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi).

parole.significato: Tone, condition.
parole.testo: From New Latin -tonia, from Ancient Greek -τονία (-tonía) (in ἀτονία (atonía)), from τόνος (tónos) + -ία (-ía). Compare French -tonie, German -tonie.

parole.significato: Having a trema (hole or aperture) or tremata of the type, position or number specified by the prefix.
parole.testo: From New Latin trēma (“aperture”), from Ancient Greek τρῆμα (trêma), from Proto-Hellenic *trḗmə (“hole”), from Proto-Indo-European *tréh₁-mn̥ (“to drill”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to drill”).

parole.significato: urine; urination; presence in urine (of a substance denoted by a prefixed combining form); state or condition of the ur…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, Latin -ūria, from Ancient Greek -ουρία (-ouría), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: One of the tiles or squares of a tessellated pavement; an abaculus.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀβακίσκος (abakískos, “a coloured stone for laying mosaic”), diminutive of ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”). See abacus.

parole.significato: An inability to walk due to a defect in muscular coordination.
parole.testo: From New Latin a- (“without”) + Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, “step”) + New Latin -ia (“pathological condition”).

parole.significato: A typically malignant fatty tumor located on the trunk.
parole.testo: Named after John Abernethy, English surgeon, + New Latin, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma, “fleshy growth”), from σαρκόω (sarkóō, “become fleshy”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: An order of annelids, so called because the species composing it have no special organs of respiration, usually includi…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”) + -ata.

parole.significato: Either of the ratlike rodents that form the genus Abrocoma; rat chinchilla.
parole.testo: From New Latin abrocoma, from Ancient Greek ἁβροκόμης (habrokómēs, “with delicate hair”), from ἁβρός (habrós, “splendid, delicate”) + κόμη (kómē, “hair”).

parole.significato: Absence of willpower or decisiveness, especially as a symptom of mental illness.
parole.testo: From New Latin abūlia, from Ancient Greek ἀβουλία (aboulía, “irresolution”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + βουλή (boulḗ, “will”).

parole.significato: The garden in Athens where the academics met.
parole.testo: From New Latin academia, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía); Doublet of academia, academy, and Akademeia. parole.significato: The scientific and cultural community engaged in higher education and research, taken as a whole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attica hero Akademos. parole.significato: Having thorns.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn plant”), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”).

parole.significato: A point lying near the base of the nose; specifically, the point at the base of the anterior nasal spine that lies on t…
parole.testo: From New Latin acanthion, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”) + -ion.

parole.significato: With thorns
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn plant”), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”).

parole.significato: Any fish of the superorder Acanthopterygii.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from acanthus (“thorn”), (from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos)) + Ancient Greek πτερύγιον (pterúgion) diminutive of πτέρυξ (ptérux, “wing, fin”), from πτερόν (pterón, “feather, wing”).

parole.significato: The state in which the level of carbon dioxide in the blood and tissue is significantly lower than normal.
parole.testo: From New Latin acapnia, from Ancient Greek ἄκαπνος (ákapnos, “without smoke”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + καπνός (kapnós, “smoke”).

parole.significato: Any parasitic arachnid, such as mites and ticks, of the subclass Acarina.

parole.significato: mite
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from New Latin acarus, from Ancient Greek ἄκαρι (ákari, “cheese mite, tick”), which is conventionally associated with the adjective ἀκαρής (akarḗs, “tiny, minute”) but may also be related to κάρνος (kárnos, “louse”) or

parole.significato: Deficiency or absence of bile.
parole.testo: From New Latin acholia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).

parole.significato: A skin condition, usually of the face, that is common in adolescents. It is characterised by red pimples, and is caused…
parole.testo: From New Latin acnē, probably a corruption of Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point, top”).

parole.significato: Threadlike defensive organs, composed largely of nettling cells (cnidae), thrown out of the mouth or special pores of c…
parole.testo: From the plural of New Latin acontium, from Ancient Greek ἀκόντιον (akóntion, “little dart”).

parole.significato: The extremities: limbs, head, fingers, toes, etc.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, per above.

parole.significato: A lack or defect of the pulse.
parole.testo: From New Latin acrotismus, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, privative a) + κρότος (krótos, “a rattling, beating”) + -ismus.

parole.significato: An insect of the genus Adelges.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Adelges + -id, first attested in 1928. The Latin term is adapted from a purported Ancient Greek *ἀδελγεῖν (*adelgeîn, “to suck”), which is unattested; it is likely there was some confusion with ἀμελγεῖν (amelgeîn, “to milk, to suck up moisture, to drink”). parole.significato: Literary works not attributed to (or claimed by) an author. (Originally used as a title of collections of anonymous Gre…
parole.testo: From New Latin adespota (“anonymous literary works”), substantivised neuter plural of the adjective adespotos (“anonymous; undedicated”, of books), from Ancient Greek ἀδέσποτος (adéspotos, “anonymous”, of rumours or writings), from ἀ- (a-, “without”, alpha privative) + δεσπότης (despótēs, “master”).

parole.significato: Defective perspiration; adiaphoresis.
parole.testo: From New Latin adiapneustia, from Ancient Greek ἀδιαπνευστία (adiapneustía, “lack of perspiration”).

parole.significato: A work of adoxography.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”) (from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -graph.

parole.significato: Fine writing on a minor or trivial subject.
parole.testo: From New Latin adoxus (“absurd, paradoxical”) (from Ancient Greek ἄδοξος (ádoxos, “obscure, ignoble”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + δόξα (dóxa, “expectation”)) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “writing”).

parole.testo: From New Latin aecidium, the diminutive form of Ancient Greek αἰκίᾱ (aikíā, “injury”). parole.significato: A cuplike fruiting structure of some parasitic rust fungi that contains chains of aeciospores.
parole.testo: From New Latin aecium, from Ancient Greek αἰκίᾱ (aikíā, “injury, insult”). However Merriam-Webster relates that aecium is a back-formation from aecidium and is not related to the Greek αἰκίᾱ (aikíā). parole.significato: A copulatory organ of some male insects.
parole.testo: From New Latin aedeagus, derived from Ancient Greek αἰδοῖα (aidoîa, “private parts, pudenda”) + ἀγός (agós, “leader”), from ἄγω (ágō, “I lead”).

parole.significato: The failure of a mother (human or otherwise) to produce sufficient milk following birth.
parole.testo: From New Latin agalactia, from Ancient Greek ἀγαλακτία (agalaktía, “lack of milk”), from ἀγάλακτος (agálaktos) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, “not; without”) + γᾰ́λᾰ, γᾰ́λᾰκτος (gắlă, gắlăktos, “milk”).

parole.significato: An antidote to poison.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexiterium and its etymon Ancient Greek ἀλεξητήριον (alexētḗrion, “remedy”), from neuter of ἀλεξητήριος (alexētḗrios, “keeping off, defending”), from ἀλεξητήρ (alexētḗr, “defender, protector”) + -ιος (-ios, adjectival suffix), from extended stem of ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to ward off”) + ‑τήρ

parole.significato: Acting as an antidote to poison.
parole.testo: From New Latin alexiterius, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξητήριος (alexētḗrios, “keeping off, defending”); see Etymology 1.

parole.significato: of a different nature or kind.
parole.testo: From New Latin, based on Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, allo- + gen- + -eous.

parole.significato: A compound purgative medicine of which aloes is a chief ingredient.
parole.testo: From New Latin aloēdarium, from Ancient Greek ἀλοηδάριον (aloēdárion), from ἀλόη (alóē, “aloes”).

parole.significato: Any form of blindness that is accompanied by no obvious change to the eye; often the result of disease of the optic ner…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin amaurōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀμαύρωσις (amaúrōsis, “dimming, obscuring, amaurosis”), from ᾰ̓μαυρόω (ămauróō, “to grow dim”), from ἀμαυρός (amaurós, “dim”).

parole.significato: Absence of menstrual discharge.
parole.testo: Via New Latin from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μήν (mḗn, “month”) + -ροια (-roia, “flowing”). By surface analysis, a- + meno- + -rrhoea.

parole.significato: starch
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin amylum (whence English amylum, amyl, and amyl-/amylo-).

parole.significato: A member of a radical wing of Christians during the Protestant Reformation, with a tenet of adult baptism.
parole.testo: From New Latin anabaptista, from the Ancient Greek ἀναβαπτισμός (anabaptismós), itself from ἀνα- (ana-, “re-”) and βαπτισμός (baptismós, “baptism”), equivalent to ana- + Baptist.

parole.significato: To baptize or christen again, or to a different denomination; to rename or rechristen
parole.testo: From New Latin anabaptizāre, from Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “again”) + βᾰπτῐ́ζω (băptĭ́zō, “to baptize”). See baptize and Anabaptist.

parole.significato: A chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object.
parole.testo: From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Analyzable as ana- + chrono- + -ism.

parole.significato: To refer to, or put into, a wrong time period.
parole.testo: From anachronism + -ize. From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

parole.significato: An unstressed syllable at the start of a verse.
parole.testo: Via New Latin from Ancient Greek ἀνάκρουσις (anákrousis, “pushing up”), from ἀνακρούω (anakroúō, “I push up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + κρούω (kroúō, “I strike”).

parole.significato: The inability to feel pain.
parole.testo: From New Latin analgēsia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλγησίᾱ (analgēsíā, “want of feeling, insensibility”), from ἀνάλγητος (análgētos), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀλγέω (algéō, “feel bodily pain, suffer”) + -τος (-tos, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Any medicine, such as aspirin, that reduces pain, especially without inducing a loss of other sensation. (Contrast anes…
parole.testo: From analgesia (“absence of pain”) + -ic, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἄλγησις (álgēsis, “sense of pain”), from ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). Compare -algia.

parole.significato: A justification of an action by inevitability or necessity.
parole.testo: From New Latin anangeon, from Ancient Greek ἀναγκαῖον (anankaîon), neuter of ἀναγκαῖος (anankaîos, “necessary”). The spelling of this word with -ng- is unexpected. parole.testo: From New Latin anaptychus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπτυχος (anáptukhos, “unfolding”), from ἀναπτύσσω (anaptússō, “to unfold”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to anaptyxis; of a vowel having been inserted into a word.
parole.testo: From New Latin anaptycticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπτυκτος (anáptuktos, “that may be opened”) + -icus (adjectival suffix), from ἀνα- (ana-, “up; again; back”) + πτυκτός (ptuktós, “folded”), from the stem of πτύσσω (ptússō, “to fold”) + τός (tós, suffix forming verbal adjectives).

parole.significato: The epenthesis (insertion) of a vowel.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin anaptyxis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπτυξις (anáptuxis).

parole.significato: The state of a society being without authorities or an authoritative governing body.
parole.testo: From New Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía). By surface analysis, an- + -archy.

parole.significato: A muscle of the elbow and forearm.
parole.testo: From New Latin anconaeus, which is itself derived from an adjective formation **ἀγκωναῖος (**ankōnaîos) of Ancient Greek ἀγκών (ankṓn).

parole.significato: The set of a flower's stamens.
parole.testo: From New Latin; from andro- + oecium (from Ancient Greek οἰκῐ́ον (oikĭ́on), diminutive of οἶκος (oîkos, “house”)).

parole.significato: A robot that is designed to look and act like a human being (not necessarily a male one).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin androides, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρός (andrós, genitive of ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man, human”)) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, itself from εἶδος (eîdos, “form, image, shape, appearance, look”)). By surface analysis, andr- + -oid.

parole.significato: Dilute or disorganized energy, which cannot be transformed into work; bound energy
parole.testo: From New Latin anergia, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not, without”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: An artificial method of preventing sensation, used to eliminate pain without causing loss of vital functions, by the ad…
parole.testo: Sense of “insensibility” attested since 1679, from New Latin anaesthēsia, from Ancient Greek ἀναισθησία (anaisthēsía, “without sensation”), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) and αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “sensation”). By surface analysis, an- + -esthesia. Sense of “state induced by an agent” attested since 1846.

parole.significato: The use of a word from one word class or part of speech as if it were from another, in English typically the use of a n…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin antimeria, from Latin anti- (from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντῐ- (ăntĭ-, “opposite”)) + Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”) + Latin -ia, with non-etymological ⟨h⟩.

parole.significato: calathidium.
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: The scientific study of humans, systematically describing the ethnographic, linguistic, archaeological, and evolutionar…
parole.testo: From New Latin anthropologia, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human, mankind”) + -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, anthropo- + -logy.

parole.significato: The absence of the lens of the eye, causing hypermetropia and a loss of accommodation.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, privative prefix) + φᾰκός (phăkós, “lentil”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, noun suffix). Equivalent to a- + phakia.

parole.significato: The point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, or other astronomical object, where it is farthest from the Sun.
parole.testo: From New Latin aphēlium (whence English aphelium, now displaced) + -ion (used in the names of other apsides). parole.significato: A type of aphasia in which the ability to speak is lost or severely impaired.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin aphēmia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “voice”). By surface analysis, a- + -phemia.

parole.significato: A sap-sucking insect pest of the superfamily Aphidoidea; an aphidian.
parole.testo: From New Latin aphis (plural aphides), coined by Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus in 1758. parole.significato: Loss of voice; the inability to speak.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin aphōnia, from Ancient Greek ἀφωνία (aphōnía, “speechlessness”). By surface analysis, a- + -phonia.

parole.significato: Having no leaves; leafless.
parole.testo: 19th century, from New Latin aphyllus, from Ancient Greek ἄφυλλος (áphullos, “leafless”) (ἀ- (a-) + φύλλον (phúllon)).

parole.significato: The cessation of breathing, most often in reference to transient instances thereof during sleep.
parole.testo: From a- + -pnea, from the New Latin apnoea, from the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia), formed from ἀ- (a-, “absence of”) + πνοή (pnoḗ, “breathing”).

parole.significato: Relating to or resembling spider webs; covered with or composed of soft loose hairs or fibers.
parole.testo: Mid 18th century borrowing from New Latin arachnoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρᾰχνοειδής (ărăkhnoeidḗs, “like a cobweb”), from ᾰ̓ρᾰ́χνη (ărắkhnē, “spider web”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-oid, -like”). By surface analysis, arachn- + -oid.

parole.significato: The adoption or imitation of archaic words or style.

parole.significato: A primitive fin, like that of Ceratodus.
parole.testo: From New Latin archipterygium, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion). By surface analysis, archi- + pterygium

parole.significato: The trend in evolution towards a greater amount of organization
parole.testo: From New Latin, from aro- (from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́ρᾰ (ắră), ἄρ (ár) (“there and then, straightway”; also, interrogative and connective particle)) + morphosis.

parole.significato: An irregular heartbeat; a lack of a regular pulse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin arrhythmia, from Ancient Greek ἀρρυθμία (arrhuthmía), equivalent to a- + rhythm + -ia.

parole.significato: articulation = joint (as for example in arthroplasty).
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (árthron, “a joint”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -o-.

parole.significato: An affliction characterized by pain in or around a joint, not dependent upon structural disease like arthritis.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”).

parole.significato: An invertebrate animal of the phylum Arthropoda, characterized by a chitinous exoskeleton and multiple jointed appendag…
parole.testo: From New Latin Arthropoda, from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”) + πούς (poús, “foot”), equivalent to arthro- + -pod.

parole.significato: Bread-worship (the worship of the bread at Eucharist).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin artolatria, from Ancient Greek ἄρτος (ártos, “bread”) + Latin -latria (“worship”).

parole.significato: Relating to or being an arytenoid cartilage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin arytaenoīdēs (“ladle-shaped”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρῠταινοειδής (ărŭtainoeidḗs), from ᾰ̓ρύ̆ταινᾰ (ărú̆taină, “a ladle or cup”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: Any member of the class Ascidiacea (the sea squirts)
parole.testo: From New Latin Ascidia + -an, from Ancient Greek ἀσκίδιον (askídion, “wineskin, leather bag”).

parole.significato: A pitcher-shaped or flask-shaped organ or appendage of a plant.
parole.testo: From New Latin ascidium, from Ancient Greek ἀσκίδιον (askídion), from ἀσκός (askós, “leather bag”) + -ιδιον (-idion, “diminutive ending”).

parole.significato: A form of micrococcus, found in putrid meat infusions, occurring in peculiar masses, each of which is enclosed in a hya…

parole.significato: A person's life story, especially one published.

parole.significato: Synonym of life; Biota; all living things.

parole.significato: Excessive blennorrhea, or mucous discharge, especially as seen in gonorrhea.

parole.significato: An inordinate secretion and discharge of mucus.

parole.significato: Eyelid.

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Bromus.

parole.significato: A bronchial tube; a subdivision of the bronchus.

parole.significato: Either of two rounded lobes at the posterior base of the wing in many true flies.

parole.significato: A carpal, especially one of the series articulating with the metacarpals.

parole.significato: The group of bones that make up the wrist.

parole.significato: Purgative; inducing mental or physical catharsis.

parole.significato: A disorder with intense burning pain, type 2 of two types of complex regional pain syndrome.

parole.significato: Chronic joint pain, especially of the hip-joint.

parole.testo: From New Latin cercus, from Ancient Greek κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”).

parole.significato: Either of the prehensile claws found on the proboscis of chelicerates (horseshoe crabs, sea spiders and arachnids).

parole.significato: massage as a form of therapy

parole.significato: A funnel; a funnel-shaped opening.

parole.significato: Relating to the common bile duct.

parole.significato: A collection of written passages, used to learn an unfamiliar language.

parole.significato: film, movie, cinema (moving pictures).

parole.significato: A standard, test, or requirement by which individual things or people may be compared and judged; a gauge.

parole.significato: Any of various plants, of the genus Croton, that yield croton oil.

parole.significato: An excessive accumulation of serum in tissue spaces or a body cavity.

parole.significato: Possessing or pertaining to energy.

parole.significato: A journal or diary.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an epigraph or to epigraphy.

parole.significato: A gradual decay through slow combustion or oxidation, like that of old trees or dead animals.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Haloragaceae.

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plant genus Hamamelis, the witch hazels.

parole.significato: The middle of the posterior margin of the foramen magnum of the skull.
parole.testo: From New Latin opisthion, from Ancient Greek ὀπίσθιος (opísthios, “rear, behind”), from ὄπισθεν (ópisthen, “at the back, backwards”). By surface analysis, opisth- + -ion.

parole.significato: A plant of the orchid family (Orchidaceae), bearing unusually-shaped flowers of beautiful colours.
parole.testo: From New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) (ostensibly from the shape of the roots). Supplanted Middle English ballokwort (literally “testicle plant”).

parole.significato: The branch of zoology that deals with the scientific study of birds.
parole.testo: From New Latin ornithologia, coined by Ulisse Aldrovandi from Ancient Greek ὀρνιθολόγος (ornithológos), from ὄρνις (órnis) and λόγος (lógos). See also ornitho- + -logy.

parole.significato: Any of the armored jawless fishes of the Paleozoic.
parole.testo: From New Latin ostracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “pottery fragment; shell”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).

parole.significato: A fragment of pottery.
parole.testo: From New Latin ostracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “pottery fragment; shell”).

parole.significato: a fish with a pointed snout
parole.testo: From New Latin oxyrhynchus, from Ancient Greek ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos, “a kind of Egyptian fish”) (whence also the place name Ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (Oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos), from ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp”) + ῥῠ́γχος (rhŭ́nkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: A genus, Pachysandra, of four or five species of evergreen shrubs or subshrubs, belonging to the boxwood family, Buxace…
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name, equivalent to English pachy-, from Ancient Greek παχύς (pakhús) [Term?].

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmicticus, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: A situation in which an individual is just as likely to mate with a randomly chosen individual as any other in the popu…
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixia, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: Panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixis, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”).

parole.significato: The conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to a tangent plane to the cone; the locus…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of parable, parole, and palaver.

parole.significato: One of the two lobes forming the lower lip, or metastoma, of Crustacea.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin paragnathus, from para- + Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”). Compare earlier paragnatha.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to parallax
parole.testo: From New Latin parallacticus, from Ancient Greek παραλλακτικός (parallaktikós).

parole.significato: A parallelopiped.
parole.testo: From New Latin parallelopipedon, alteration of Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

parole.significato: A condition where the lower half of a patient's body is paralyzed and cannot move.
parole.testo: From New Latin paraplegia, from Ancient Greek παραπληγίη (paraplēgíē), Ionic Greek for παραπληξία (paraplēxía, “paralysis on one side”), from παραπλήσσεσθαι (paraplḗssesthai, “to be stricken on one side”), active παραπλήσσειν (paraplḗssein, “to strike on one side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + πλήσ

parole.significato: A paralysis which is incomplete or which occurs in isolated areas.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πάρεσις (páresis, “letting go, paralysis”), from παρίημι (paríēmi, “relax”), from παρα- (para-) + ἵημι (híēmi, “let go”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Peperomia, some of which are popular houseplants.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin peperomia, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”) + ὅμοιος (hómoios, “similar, like”).

parole.significato: The outer layer that covers the spore-bearing organ in many fungi.
parole.testo: A New Latin form of Ancient Greek πηρίδιον (pērídion, “little pouch”).

parole.significato: A specialized sheath-like bract that surrounds the ovary or fruit of some flowering plants, especially those in the fam…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perigynium, from peri- + Ancient Greek γῠνή (gŭnḗ, “woman”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A petal.
parole.testo: From New Latin petalum, from Ancient Greek πέταλον (pétalon), from πέταλος (pétalos, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Hellenic *pétalos, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out”). Doublet of petal.

parole.significato: Any of three small wading birds in the genus Phalaropus, of the family Scolopacidae, that have lobed toes.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phalaropus, formed irregularly from Ancient Greek φαλαρίς (phalarís, “coot”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: Forms terms relating to the pharynx.
parole.testo: From New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx, “throat”), akin to modern Greek φάρυγγας (fáryngas, “pharynx”).

parole.significato: The part of the alimentary canal and respiratory tract that extends from the back of the mouth and nasal cavity to the…
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φᾰ́ρῠγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat”).

parole.significato: A distinguishable part of a sequence or cycle occurring over time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin phasis, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”), from φᾰ(ν)- (phă(n)-, root of φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light; to appear”)) + -σῐς (-sĭs). Compare phantasm and see face.

parole.significato: Any of several climbing plants, of the genus Philodendron, native to America and the West Indies that are often grown a…
parole.testo: From New Latin philodendron, from Ancient Greek φῐλόδενδρον (phĭlódendron), neuter of φῐλόδενδρος (phĭlódendros, “loving trees”). First known use: 1877.

parole.significato: An inflammation, especially of the internal organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φλεγμᾰσία (phlegmăsía, “inflammation”), from φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame”) (whence also phlegm).

parole.significato: The hypothetical fiery principle formerly assumed to be a necessary constituent of combustible bodies and to be given u…
parole.testo: From New Latin phlogiston, coined by Georg Ernst Stahl in 1702, from Ancient Greek φλογιστόν (phlogistón), neuter of φλογιστός (phlogistós, “burnt up, inflammable”), from φλογίζω (phlogízō, “to set fire to”), from φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Phlox.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phlox, from Ancient Greek φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: An irrational, abnormal, or obsessive fear (of something).
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the diaphragm
parole.testo: From New Latin phrenicus, from Ancient Greek φρήν (phrḗn, “diaphragm”).

parole.significato: A local division of the people; a clan or tribe.
parole.testo: From New Latin phȳlē, from Ancient Greek φῡλή (phūlḗ, “a union of individuals into a community”).

parole.significato: phyllode
parole.testo: From New Latin phyllōdium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “leaflike”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Physalis.
parole.testo: From New Latin Physalis, coined by Linnaeus from Ancient Greek φυσαλλίς (phusallís, “bladder, wind instrument”), from φυσιόω (phusióō, “to puff up, blow up”), φυσώ (phusṓ).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Phytolacca of herbaceous plants; the poke or pokeweed.
parole.testo: From New Latin phytolacca, from Ancient Greek φῠτόν (phŭtón, “plant”) + Italian lacca (“crimson lake”).

parole.significato: A plant-like animal; a zoophyte.
parole.testo: From phyto- + zoon, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A procedure in which whole blood is removed from a donor or patient and centrifuged to isolate blood cells that are res…
parole.testo: From New Latin plasma + Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “removal”).

parole.significato: A semiaquatic monotreme from eastern Australia with a bill resembling that of a duck, that has a mole-like body, a tail…
parole.testo: From New Latin Platypus (originally a genus name already in use for a type of beetle), from Ancient Greek πλατύπους (platúpous, “flat-footed”), from πλατύς (platús, “flat”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of flatfoot.

parole.significato: A superficial muscle of the human neck that overlaps the sternocleidomastoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin platysma, from Ancient Greek πλᾰ́τῠσμᾰ (plắtŭsmă, “flat object”), from πλᾰτῠ́νω (plătŭ́nō, “widen”) + -μᾰ (-mă, “nominal suffix”).

parole.significato: The study of the respiratory system and organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin pneumologia, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, pneumo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A nocturnal monster in Ancient Greece that would choke its victims; incubus; nightmare.
parole.testo: From New Latin pnīgalion, from Ancient Greek πνῑγαλίων (pnīgalíōn, “nightmare”), from πνῑ́γω (pnī́gō, “to throttle, strangle”).

parole.significato: A stalk which bears the fructification in some lichens, such as the reindeer moss.
parole.testo: From New Latin podetium, from Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: A solid figure with many flat faces and straight edges.
parole.testo: From New Latin polyedron, from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”); compare French polyèdre. By surface analysis, poly- + -hedron.

parole.significato: Having, or assuming, a variety of forms, characters, or styles
parole.testo: From New Latin polymorphus, from Ancient Greek πολύμορφος (polúmorphos, “multiform, manifold”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many, much”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). By surface analysis, poly- + -morphous.

parole.significato: Inability of the eye, due to ageing, to focus on nearby objects.
parole.testo: From New Latin presbyōpia, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old man”), and New Latin -ōpia (“vision problem”), from Ancient Greek ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”). By surface analysis, presby- + -opia.

parole.significato: A waterspout.
parole.testo: From New Latin prēstēr, from Ancient Greek πρηστήρ (prēstḗr, “hurricane or waterspout attended with lightning; (in plural) veins of the neck when swollen by anger”).

parole.significato: The addition of a leap day to the lunar calendar.
parole.testo: From New Latin proemptōsis, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “before”) + ἔμπτωσις (émptōsis, “falling”).

parole.significato: Being the product of two consecutive integers.
parole.testo: Apparently from New Latin pronicus, a misspelling of Latin promicus, from Ancient Greek προμήκης (promḗkēs, “elongated, oblong”), but the spelling has been pronic from its earliest known occurrence in English (Leonhard Euler, Opera Omnia, series 1, volume 15).

parole.significato: An early larval form of a trematode worm; a redia.
parole.testo: From New Latin proscōlēx, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-) + σκώληξ (skṓlēx).

parole.significato: Artificial, acting as a substitute for part of the body; relating to prosthesis.
parole.testo: From New Latin prostheticus, from Ancient Greek προσθετικός (prosthetikós, “adding; repletive; giving additional power”), from πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -etic.

parole.significato: Divination by drawing pebbles from a pile.
parole.testo: From New Latin psēphomantia, from Ancient Greek ψῆφος (psêphos, “pebble used for casting a vote”), + -mancy.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or lying in the region of the inferior part of the sphenoid bone of the vertebrate skull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pterygoīdēs, from Ancient Greek πτερῠγοειδής (pterŭgoeidḗs, “like a wing”), from πτέρῠξ (ptérŭx, “a wing”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: The appearance or study of feathers on a bird, including factors such as their texture or shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilōsis, from the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λωσῐς (ptĭ́lōsĭs).

parole.significato: The way in which an individual leaf is folded in the bud.
parole.testo: From New Latin ptyxis, from Ancient Greek πτύξις (ptúxis, “a folding”).

parole.significato: The passage between the iter and optocoele in the brain.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyla, from Ancient Greek πύλη (púlē, “gate, entrance”).

parole.significato: pus
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πύον (púon, “pus”), from Proto-Indo-European *puH-; compare Sanskrit पूयति (pūyati, “stinks, rots”), Ancient Greek πύθω (púthō, “to rot”), Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌻𐍃 (fuls, “foul”), Old English ful (“foul”).

parole.significato: A nutlet resembling a seed, or the stone of a drupe, comprising the endocarp and the kernel.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyrēna, from Ancient Greek πῡρήν (pūrḗn, “fruit-stone”).

parole.significato: Caused by, pertaining to or resulting in fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pyreticus, from Ancient Greek πυρετικός (puretikós, “febrile”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.testo: From New Latin acidum pyruvicum, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ūva (“grape”) + -icum (neuter singular of -icus), from its being produced by the dry distillation of racemic acid, originally derived from grapes. By surface analysis, pyr(e) + Latin uv(a) + -ic.

parole.significato: A seed capsule in the form of a box, the seeds being released when the top splits off.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πυξίδιον (puxídion), diminutive of πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s, “box”).

parole.significato: The spinal column, or the vertebrae of the spine.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhachis/rachis, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”).

parole.significato: A seamlike ridge or furrow on an organ, bodily tissue, or other structure, typically marking the line where two halves…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin raphē, from Ancient Greek ῥᾰφή (rhăphḗ, “seam; suture”).

parole.significato: A simple, straight spicule.
parole.testo: From a New Latin form of Ancient Greek ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”).

parole.significato: Compulsive nose-picking; the insertion of a finger into one's nose.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Rhipsalis, epiphytic flowering plants in the cactus family, often known as mistletoe cacti.

parole.significato: One of the small sensory tentacular structures of various jellyfish species.

parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”) + -cercous.

parole.significato: A trumpet-shaped tube.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin salpinx.

parole.significato: Either of two species of osteoglossid fish of the genus Scleropages, native to northeastern Australia.
parole.testo: Origin unknown. Perhaps a mispronunciation of New Latin Ceratodus (“an extinct genus of lungfish”), which is from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”).

parole.testo: From New Latin scatophagus, from Ancient Greek σκατοφάγος (skatophágos), from σκατο- (skato-, “shit”) and φάγος (phágos, “eater; glutton”), from φᾰγεῖν (phăgeîn, “to eat”) + -ος (-os, “-er”, forming agent nouns). parole.testo: From New Latin scatophagus, from Ancient Greek σκατοφάγος (skatophágos), from σκατο- (skato-, “shit”) and φάγος (phágos, “eating”), from φᾰγεῖν (phăgeîn, “to eat”) + -ος (-os, “-ous”, forming adjectives). Equivalent to scato- + -phagous.

parole.significato: A scholium.
parole.testo: From New Latin scholion, from Ancient Greek σχόλῐον (skhólĭon, “interpretation, comment”).

parole.significato: A note added to a text as an explanation, criticism or commentary.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion, “comment”), from σχολή (skholḗ, “discussion”).

parole.significato: The white of the eye; the tough outer coat of the eye that covers the eyeball except for the cornea.

parole.significato: A chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by hardening the skin or other organs through excessive deposits of…
parole.testo: From New Latin sclēroderma, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”). By surface analysis, sclero- + -derma.

parole.significato: A compact mass of hardened mycelium stored with reserve food material that, in some higher fungi such as ergot, becomes…
parole.testo: From New Latin sclerotium, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

parole.significato: Semiotics, the study of signs.
parole.testo: From New Latin semaeologia, from Ancient Greek σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “sign”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, semio- + -logy.

parole.significato: Synonym of septicemia.
parole.testo: From New Latin septaemia, from Ancient Greek σηπτός (sēptós), verbal adjective of σήπω (sḗpō, “make rotten”), + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ia.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Sittidae, or nuthatches.
parole.testo: From New Latin sitta (“the nuthatch”), from Ancient Greek σίττη (síttē, “nuthatch”) + -ine.

parole.significato: To reduce to a skeleton; to skin; to skeletonize.

parole.significato: The whole axial portion of an animal, including the head, neck, trunk, and tail.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: Any reproductive structure, in some lichens and fungi, that produces spores.
parole.testo: From New Latin sōrus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a spasm; resembling a sudden contraction of the muscles.
parole.testo: From New Latin spasmōdicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (spasmṓdēs, “spasmodic”), from σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Spathiphyllum of peace lilies.
parole.testo: From New Latin, shortening of the genus name Spathiphyllum, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”) + φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: Having a wedge shape.
parole.testo: From New Latin sphenoides, from Ancient Greek σφηνοειδής (sphēnoeidḗs, “wedge-shaped”), from σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-form, -like”).

parole.significato: Any of the many flowering shrubs of the genus Spiraea, that have clusters of white or pink flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “coil”).

parole.significato: Of, in, near or pertaining to the viscera or intestines.
parole.testo: From New Latin splanchnicus, from Ancient Greek σπλαγχνικός (splankhnikós), from σπλάγχνα (splánkhna, “viscera”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: A reproductive particle, usually a single cell, released by a fungus, alga, or plant that may germinate into another.
parole.testo: From New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”), related to σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”). Related to English spread).

parole.significato: A secondary spore borne on a promycelium, or a filament produced from a spore, in certain kinds of minute fungi.
parole.testo: From New Latin sporidium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + -idium.

parole.significato: In flowering plants, a male reproductive structure in a flower that produces pollen, typically consisting of an anther…

parole.significato: An abortive stamen, or any organ modified from an abortive stamen; a staminodium
parole.testo: From New Latin stāminōdium, from Latin stāmen (“warp, thread”) + Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”).

parole.significato: A slackening or arrest of the blood current, due not to a lessening of the heart’s beat, but to some abnormal resistanc…
parole.testo: From New Latin stasis, from Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis). See the doublet stead.

parole.significato: steatopygia
parole.testo: From New Latin steatopyga, from Ancient Greek στέᾱτος (stéātos). See steato-, pygo-.

parole.significato: Pertaining to steatopygia; having fat or prominent buttocks.
parole.testo: From steatopyga, steatopygia + -ous. Steatopyga is borrowed from New Latin steatopyga, from Ancient Greek στέᾱτος (stéātos) (genitive singular of στέαρ (stéar, “hard fat, suet, tallow”)) + πῡγή (pūgḗ, “buttocks, rump”).

parole.significato: An abnormal narrowing or stricture in a blood vessel or other tubular organ.
parole.testo: From New Latin stenōsis, from Ancient Greek στένωσις (sténōsis, “narrowing”), from στενόω (stenóō, “to confine, to contract”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix), equivalent to steno- + -osis.

parole.significato: A special pod-like or fusiform branch containing tetraspores, found in certain red algae.
parole.testo: From New Latin stichidium, from Ancient Greek στιχίδιον (stikhídion), by surface analysis, sticho- + -idium.

parole.significato: One of the tiny pores in the epidermis of a leaf or stem through which gases and water vapor pass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin stoma, from Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: The region of a sporangium where dehiscence takes place
parole.testo: From New Latin stomium, from Ancient Greek στόμιον (stómion), from στόμα (stóma) + -ιον (-ion).

parole.significato: A defect of vision in which one eye cannot focus with the other on an object because of imbalance of the eye muscles; a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin strabismus, from Ancient Greek στραβισμός (strabismós), from στραβίζω (strabízō, “to squint”), from στραβός (strabós, “squinting”) (whence the synonymous Latin strabus).

parole.significato: A jointed series of segments of an organism, as of the body of a tapeworm, posterior to the unjointed collum.
parole.testo: From New Latin strobila, from Ancient Greek στροβίλη (strobílē).

parole.significato: A collective fleshy fruit, in which the ovaries are hidden within a hollow receptacle, as in the fig; a hollow ball wit…
parole.testo: From New Latin sȳconium, from Ancient Greek σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + -ium.

parole.significato: The divided part beyond the pylangium in the aortic trunk of the amphibian heart.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from syn- + Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “a vessel”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a synapse—the junction between the terminal of a neuron and another cell.
parole.testo: From New Latin synapticus, from Ancient Greek συναπτικός (sunaptikós, “capable of adjusting”).

parole.significato: A recognizable pattern of signs, symptoms and/or behaviours, especially of a disease or medical or psychological condit…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ, “concurrence of symptoms, concourse”), from σύνδρομος (súndromos, “running together”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + δρόμος (drómos, “running, course”).

parole.significato: Synonym of thesaurus.
parole.testo: From New Latin synōnymicon, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía, “synonym”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a synopsis.
parole.testo: From New Latin synopticus, from Ancient Greek συνοπτικός (sunoptikós, “seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from σύνοψις (súnopsis, “a general view, synopsis”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).

parole.significato: Of, related to or connected with syntax.
parole.testo: From New Latin syntacticus, from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós).

parole.significato: A change in the structure of magma by melting or the assimilation of a different type of rock.
parole.testo: From New Latin syntēxis, from Ancient Greek σύντηξις (súntēxis, “a melting”).

parole.significato: The rhythmic contraction of the heart, by which blood is driven through the arteries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek συστολή (sustolḗ), from συστέλλω (sustéllō, “to contract”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”).

parole.significato: A rapid resting heart rate, especially one above 100 beats per minute; palpitations.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin tachycardia, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (takhús, “swift”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”). By surface analysis, tachy- + -cardia. Compare French tachycardie.

parole.significato: A maneuver, or action calculated to achieve some end.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin tactica, from Ancient Greek τακτικός (taktikós, “fit for ordering”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to order, to arrange”).

parole.significato: A marine bivalve mollusc, of the genus Tellina, that burrows in the sand, from where it siphons detritus.
parole.testo: From New Latin Tellina, from Ancient Greek τελλίνη (tellínē, “a small bivalve shellfish”)

parole.significato: Inflammation of a tendon.
parole.testo: From New Latin from tendin-, stem of Medieval Latin tendo, from Late Latin tenon, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “tendon, sinew”). By surface analysis, tendon + -itis and tendo- + -itis but not actually formed in this way; similarly with tendinopathy § Etymology.

parole.significato: The hymenium
parole.testo: From New Latin thēcium, from Ancient Greek θήκιον (thḗkion), diminutive of θήκη (thḗkē, “sheath”).

parole.significato: The tip or peak of a nipple.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”) + -ion. By surface analysis, thel- + -ion.

parole.significato: A nipple or papilla.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”). By surface analysis, thel- + -ium.

parole.significato: A surveying instrument, consisting of a small mounted telescope, used to measure horizontal and vertical angles.
parole.testo: From New Latin theodolitus (1571), perhaps containing Ancient Greek θέᾱ (théā, “sight, view”) and Arabic العِضَادَة (al-ʕiḍāda, “astrolabe, alidade”); if so, doublet of alidade.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to therapy.

parole.significato: Attempted remediation of a health problem following a diagnosis, usually synonymous with treatment.
parole.testo: From New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “to serve, treat medically”) + -ία (-ía, suffix for forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Compression, especially constriction of vessels by an external cause.
parole.testo: From New Latin thlipsis, from Ancient Greek θλῖψις (thlîpsis, “pressure”).

parole.significato: A hymn to Dionysus, sung in processions in his honour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thriambus, from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of triumph and trump.

parole.significato: thrombus
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Greek the Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “lump”, “piece”, “blood clot”, “milk curd”).

parole.significato: A blood clot formed from platelets and other elements that forms in a blood vessel in a living organism, and causes thr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thrombus, from the Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “lump, piece, blood clot, milk curd”); compare thrombo-.

parole.significato: A tree of the genus Thuja.
parole.testo: From taxonomic New Latin Thuja, from Ancient Greek θυία (thuía).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being the thyroid cartilage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin thyreoīdēs, from Ancient Greek θῠρεοειδής (thŭreoeidḗs, “shield-shaped”), from θῠρεός (thŭreós, “an oblong shield”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-form, -like”).

parole.significato: The cutting edge of the bill of a bird.
parole.testo: From New Latin tomium, from Ancient Greek τομός (tomós, “sharp”) + -ium. See -tome.

parole.significato: affected by or otherwise relating to toxemia, organically poisoned
parole.testo: From toxemia (“organic blood poisoning”) + -ic, from New Latin toxaemia, from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón, “poison, toxin”) + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: An infectious disease of the eyelid caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
parole.testo: From New Latin trachōma, from Ancient Greek τράχωμα (trákhōma, “roughness”), from τρᾱχύς (trākhús, “rough”) + -ωμα (-ōma).

parole.significato: A (convex) quadrilateral with two (non-adjacent) parallel sides.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin trapezoïdēs. By surface analysis, trapeze + -oid. First attested in 1704.

parole.significato: Any of several parasitic roundworms, of the genus Trichinella, that infect the intestines and cause trichinosis
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχινος (tríkhinos, “of hair”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: Ingrown eyelash; trichiasis.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχωμα (tríkhōma), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) + -μα (-ma). Doublet of trichome.

parole.significato: The branch of mathematics that deals with the relationships between the sides and angles of (in particular) right-angle…
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to trigono- + -metry.

parole.significato: trituration
parole.testo: From New Latin trīpsis, from Ancient Greek τρῖψις (trîpsis, “rubbing, friction”), from τρῑ́βω (trī́bō, “I rub”).

parole.significato: The inability to open the mouth normally, typically as a result of disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin trismus, from Ancient Greek τρισμός (trismós, “a grinding, rasping, scream”), from Ancient Greek τρίζω (trízō).

parole.significato: A radioactive isotope of the element hydrogen (symbol T, ³H or 31H) having one proton and two neutrons.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin tritium, from Ancient Greek τρίτος (trítos, “third”) + New Latin -ium. By surface analysis, trit- + -ium.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Trochus, or more generally of the family Trochidae; in non-specialist usage, including species…
parole.testo: From New Latin Trochus, from Ancient Greek τροχός (trokhós, “wheel”).

parole.significato: One of the soft pads on the undersurface of the toes of some birds, such as owls and ospreys.
parole.testo: From New Latin tylarus, from Ancient Greek τυλάριον (tulárion, “cushion”).

parole.significato: Any of several similar diseases, characterised by high recurrent fever, caused by Rickettsia bacteria. Not to be confus…
parole.testo: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-, extended form of *dʰew- (“scatter like dust”).

parole.significato: A band of fibrous tissue extending from the bladder to the umbilicus.
parole.testo: From New Latin ūrachus, from Ancient Greek οὐραχός (ourakhós).

parole.significato: ureter.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek οὐρητήρ (ourētḗr). By surface analysis, ureter + -o-.

parole.significato: Tail.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: A median ossification at the back of the lophosteon in the sternum of some birds.
parole.testo: From New Latin ūrosteon, from Ancient Greek οὐρᾱ́ (ourā́, “tail”) + ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).

parole.significato: A deposit of cholesterol on the eyelid.
parole.testo: From New Latin xanthelasma, from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + ἔλασμα (élasma, “metal plate, foil”).

parole.significato: The concept of hospitality to strangers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin xenia, from Ancient Greek ξενῐ́ᾱ (xenĭ́ā, “hospitality”).

parole.significato: One who believed that maize was the cause of pellagra.
parole.testo: From New Latin zea, from Ancient Greek ζειά (zeiá, “spelt”), + -ist.

parole.significato: One of the cells or tubes which enclose the feeding zooids of Bryozoa.
parole.testo: From New Latin zōoecium, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A distinct organism.
parole.testo: First adopted by Herbert Spencer in Principles of Biology (see 1864 quotation): from New Latin zōon, from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

parole.significato: A larval stage of certain decapod crustaceans, especially of decapods such as crabs and certain Anomura, also called th…
parole.testo: From New Latin zōaea, zōēa, from Ancient Greek ζωή (zōḗ, “life”) (compare ζῷον (zōîon)).
